deep.reconstruction:
Context: this page finishes an estimate begun on the previous page (paragraph marked (61)). That paragraph matches the localization argument in Riemann's Habilitationsschrift on trigonometric series (1854, publ. 1867). There, mu^2 times an integral of F(x) cos mu(x-a) lambda(x) is expanded termwise. The coefficients are bounded by mu^2/((mu-n)^2 n^2) for the terms n lying outside two bounded windows -c' < n < c'' and mu-c''' < n < mu+c^IV, with all c > 1. Writing t = n/mu gives sum mu^2/((mu-n)^2 n^2) = (1/mu) sum (1/mu)/((1-t)^2 t^2). The integrand has no interior maximum, so a lower-step (Riemann-sum) comparison bounds this sum by (1/mu) times the integral of dx/(x^2(1-x)^2). The integral runs over (-inf, -(c'-1)/mu], [(c''-1)/mu, 1-(c'''-1)/mu] and [1+(c^IV-1)/mu, +inf).

This page:

(1) Partial fractions, worked in the side computation at the bottom of the page. Since 1/(x(1-x)) = 1/x + 1/(1-x), squaring gives 1/(x^2(1-x)^2) = 1/x^2 + 1/(1-x)^2 + 2/(x(1-x)). The cross term is again 2/(x(1-x)) = 2/x + 2/(1-x).

(2) Integration: (1/mu) * integral dx/(x^2(1-x)^2) = (1/mu)(-1/x + 1/(1-x) + 2 log x - 2 log(1-x)) + Const.

(3) Conclusion: between the stated limits this has a value that does not become infinite with mu. Implicit step (mine): at x = (c''-1)/mu the term -1/x contributes mu/(c''-1). After the prefactor 1/mu this is the bounded quantity 1/(c''-1); the same holds at the other three finite endpoints. The logarithmic terms contribute O(log mu / mu), which tends to 0. At x = ±infinity, -1/x + 1/(1-x) tends to 0 and log|x/(1-x)| tends to 0. Hence the tail sum is O(1) as mu grows, roughly sum over the endpoints of 1/(c-1). This is what the localization argument needs.
errors: No substantive error. Minor: the antiderivative should use log|x| and log|1-x|, since the ranges include x<0 and x>1; Riemann writes log x and log(1-x). The difference is harmless because only differences over intervals not containing 0 or 1 are taken.
The bound requires c > 1 so that the endpoints (c-1)/mu are positive; this matches the hypothesis on the previous page ('wenn die Grössen c > 1 sind').

results.what: Partial fraction decomposition 1/(x^2(1-x)^2) = 1/x^2 + 1/(1-x)^2 + 2/x + 2/(1-x) and its antiderivative
Bounding the tail sum of mu^2/((mu-n)^2 n^2), over n away from 0 and mu, by an integral that stays bounded as mu grows
results.modern_name: Integral comparison (Riemann-sum) estimate within the proof of Riemann's localization principle for trigonometric series
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann, Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854, publ. 1867)

deep.surprise_reason: This is an elementary integration step in a draft of an estimate that appears in Riemann's published Habilitationsschrift (localization principle). Nothing goes beyond known material.

checkable.asserts: The partial fraction decomposition 1/(x^2(1-x)^2) = 1/x^2 + 1/(1-x)^2 + 2/x + 2/(1-x); the result should be 0.
Riemann's antiderivative is correct; the result should be 0.
The identity 1/(x(1-x)) = 1/x + 1/(1-x), squared, used for the decomposition; the result should be 0.
At the lower inner endpoint x=(c-1)/mu the contribution tends to the finite value -1/(c-1), i.e. it is bounded in mu (assume c>1).
The antiderivative (with absolute values) tends to 0 at infinity, so the infinite tails contribute finite amounts.

In the integrand denominator, the exponent on x appears overwritten (x^2), and the (1-x) factor was enclosed and then squared; the reading x^2(1-x)^2 is correct.
Line 4 reads 'und folglich zwischen den obigen Grenzen einen Werth,' with no doubtful words; the [?] marks can be removed.

The bottom scratch line is a partial-fraction side computation: 1/x^2 + 1/(1-x)^2 + 2/(x(1-x)), with 2/(x(1-x)) expanded as 2/x + 2/(1-x). The opening parenthesis around 2/(x(1-x)) marks the term being expanded.
